#2743. NFL Power Rankings entering Week 9: Broncos are 6-2 but need to improve, perhaps with some pre-deadline trades

NFC East: Cowboys | Giants | Eagles | Commanders NFC North: Bears | Lions | Packers | Vikings NFC South: Falcons | Panthers | Saints | Buccaneers NFC West: Cardinals | Rams | 49ers | Seahawks

AFC East: Bills | Dolphins | Patriots | Jets AFC North: Ravens | Bengals | Browns | Steelers AFC South: Texans | Colts | Jaguars | Titans AFC West: Broncos | Chiefs | Raiders | Chargers

The Denver Broncos went 14-3 last season with an inordinate amount of wins in close games. Everyone said that was unsustainable and they were due for regression.

This season, the Broncos are 6-2 with an inordinate amount of wins in close games. Take that, regression police.

Somehow, the Broncos are again pulling off what should be impossible. On Sunday they came back from a 24-13 deficit in the fourth quarter to beat the Kansas City Chiefs, who have had their own fortunate run in close games. It was the Broncos' 15th straight win in games decided by eight points or less, tying the 2008-09 Indianapolis Colts for the NFL record, according to ESPN Insights.

One of two things has to be true: The Broncos are incredibly lucky in games that shouldn't be far off a 50-50 proposition and that's bound to flip, or they have some skill in winning close games that nobody else has possessed aside from Peyton Manning's Colts more than 15 years ago. Regardless of how they've gotten to their impressive record, Denver has overtaken Kansas City for the best chance to win the AFC West at 56.4%, according to DVOA.

"I think honestly, to answer that, I think it has to come from, well, we did it before," Broncos head coach Sean Payton said about winning close games, according to the team's transcripts. "Then there's a belief that can get stronger and then there's experience and then you're seasoned a little, but we still have a lot of things to fix. I honestly think that's where I believe it comes from."

If the Broncos decide they are on a heater in which the coin is repeatedly flipping on their side for a statistically improbable reason, they have some work to do before the trade deadline on Nov. 10. The offense, which has been inconsistent all season and was catching boos from the home crowd Sunday after three straight three-and-outs to start the second half, should be the focus.

Denver is just 30th in yards gained this season. A play-calling change from offensive coordinator Davis Webb to Payton hasn't helped much. The Broncos aren't getting a quarterback to replace Bo Nix but practically every other position group could be a candidate for an upgrade. The defense is good enough for a long playoff run, as it was last season. The variable is the offense.

Or maybe it just doesn't matter. The Broncos have beaten the odds for two seasons. They're 20-5 since the start of the 2025 season and 16 of those wins have been by eight points or less. They continue to laugh at the regression proclamations.

Here are the NFL power rankings after Week 8 of the NFL season, looking at the biggest need for each team before the trade deadline:

The Chargers' season is lost, so the obvious move is to trade veterans who can help elsewhere. Mack is clearly at the top of that list. He has started all seven games, has three sacks and can add immediate legitimacy to a defense from the edge. He's a likely future Hall of Famer and while he isn't quite the same player at age 35, he's still an asset. He's also no stranger to being traded, having been dealt from the Raiders to the Bears and then the Bears to the Chargers earlier in his career.

"You've got to be where your feet are man, ultimately," Mack said, via Eric Williams of Fox Sports. "That can be the most difficult thing when you're dealing with a lot of outside noise and stuff. Just trying to be where your feet are at all time. That's kind of been my thing in years past."

Biggest need: Get value for Jonathan Taylor

The way the Colts gave up on Sunday, they probably should have made Taylor inactive. Everyone knows they're going to try to trade him after shipping off guard Quenton Nelson and defensive lineman DeForest Buckner. The Colts need to restock their draft picks after a regrettable trade that sent two first-round picks, including their 2027 first, to the Jets for cornerback Sauce Gardner. And, presumably, they feel some obligation to find a good home for Taylor, who has been a tremendous player for them through the years.

There will be plenty of teams, perhaps the Giants, Broncos, Packers and Vikings among them, talking about trading for Taylor, so the Colts should get a good return.

"And you know that day always comes for many players,'' Taylor said about the possibility of being traded last week, via Fox 59. "Whether you like it or not, the day may come. You may get lucky enough to stay somewhere forever, but you understand the business of it.

Others, like defensive tackle Grover Stewart and receiver Josh Downs, could be traded too. It's going to be a rough rest of the season for Indianapolis.

Biggest need: Hang onto Garrett Wilson and others

The Jets are in a great spot. If the NFL Draft was today, they'd have the fourth pick from the Colts (Sauce Gardner trade), their own pick at No. 6 and the 10th pick from the Cowboys (Quinnen Williams trade). That would be historic.

Unlike last season, when the Jets were willing to deal young players for a stockpile of picks, the right move seems to be holding onto some foundational pieces. The one that would generate a ton of interest is Wilson, who has mostly been wasted away with the Jets. But he's 26 years old, signed through 2030, and is a legitimate No. 1 receiver. Perhaps there's a minor move to be made, like trading cornerback Nahshon Wright, but the Jets already did their trading work with the 2027 draft in mind and now it's time to stand pat.

Biggest need: Trade Moro Ojomo, maybe Saquon Barkley, and many others

Howie Roseman might be the busiest general manager with the trade deadline coming up. He usually does well in trades — we'll ignore that he traded two third-round picks for two tackles and zero sacks from Jonathan Greenard so far this season — and he has plenty of assets to move.

Barkley is the most interesting figure, even as the team reportedly won't move him. A trade would make too much sense for the Eagles to not entertain any inquiries. Any team that gets him would be gambling because Barkley has been injured most of the season and his numbers are way down since his magical (and high usage) 2024 season. Multiple teams are in need of a playmaking running back. It'll be interesting to see if the Eagles' stance on Barkley changes in the next week. The bigger piece might be Ojomo, a good defensive tackle who is about to be a free agent. The Eagles could keep him and try to re-sign him, but they have a lot of money invested at defensive tackle. Tight end Dallas Goedert, edge rusher Nolan Smith and cornerback Riq Woolen are others who should be available for the right price.

It would be surprising if the Eagles aren't very active.

Biggest need: Find draft picks for some aging vets

Once the Titans traded defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to the Bears, it was a sign that any veteran was available. And the Titans have a few who don't fit in the long-term plans.

Given the hot streak running back Tony Pollard has been on, he has emerged as perhaps the most intriguing piece. Receiver Calvin Ridley is buried on the depth chart but some team could take a shot on him for a third-day draft pick. Safety Amani Hooker, who is 28 years old, has been tremendous. Edge rusher Jermaine Johnson II, in the final year of his deal, could be moved too. The Titans could have a ton of extra draft picks by the time the deadline is done.

Biggest need: Figure out what to do with Zach Sieler

Sieler has been a productive defensive tackle for many years, but he's also 31 years old. Still, the Dolphins haven't entertained trade talks for him, according to SI.com. Miami is in full rebuild mode and while Sieler helps the Dolphins now, a 1-6 team should be looking for the future, and trading a 31-year-old defensive lineman who still would have plenty of trade value makes sense. We'll see what the Dolphins do.

Trading offensive tackle Austin Jackson has also been speculated, and teams are always looking for line help. The stripped-down Dolphins roster doesn't have a lot of attractive veteran trade candidates, which makes the decision on Sieler that much more important.

Biggest need: Figuring out if they're buyers or sellers

A 2-5, last-place team should not be thinking about buying. But most teams don't have the luxury of playing in the NFC South, where 2-5 is just a game out of first place. There are pieces the Saints could trade and easily absorb the loss, like running back Kendre Miller and safety Justin Reid. Perhaps that's a way to straddle the line of competing for a division title and thinking toward the future. The Saints also should be getting running back Travis Etienne Jr. and rookie receiver Jordyn Tyson back from injuries as soon as this week, so that will feel like a pair of deadline acquisitions.

The Saints are very much in the race in a bad division. They're also early in a rebuild and their record indicates they're still in need of draft picks and young talent. That makes it a challenge to figure out what to do before the deadline.

Biggest need: Adding to the defense, maybe

At some point the Cowboys need to have an honest conversation about themselves, which seems impossible after team owner Jerry Jones proclaimed everyone is letting head coach Brian Schottenheimer down. Jones has talked about making big trades, and already made one in-season for cornerback Joey Porter Jr. A putrid defense that let Gardner Minshew tear it apart in the fourth quarter and overtime on Sunday needs a lot of help. But, is a team that has losses at home to a Buccaneers team led by an undrafted rookie quarterback and to a Cardinals team that came back from a 14-point deficit in the fourth quarter really a defensive piece away from contending for a Super Bowl? Probably not.

It puts the Cowboys in a weird place. They're not out of the NFC East race because the division isn't good. They're also not very good themselves. It's not even outlandish for the Cowboys to look in the mirror after that hideous loss to the Cardinals and admit they should be sellers. That would require self-awareness, which isn't abundant in Dallas.

Biggest need: Making a move on two defensive standouts

The Cardinals should be feeling good about themselves after a win at Dallas, their third upset road win of the season. They should also be realistic. The Cardinals aren't going to compete for a playoff spot. The progress is great but it's still a rebuild. That makes them an interesting seller.

The top trade candidate is probably edge rusher Josh Sweat, who came over from the Eagles after helping Philadelphia win a Super Bowl and hasn't had a ton of impact on a non-contending team. There's also a question about safety Budda Baker, one of Arizona's best players but is 30 years old and signed through only 2027. Both of those players could fetch valuable draft picks in a deal.

There's also question now if quarterback Jacoby Brissett could move; he was benched on Sunday and replaced by Gardner Minshew, who has been named the starter for Week 9 vs. the Seahawks. Minshew and Carson Beck are higher priorities now. But the biggest key is finding the best return for Sweat and perhaps Baker.

Like everyone else in the NFC South and NFC East, other than the Eagles, the Commanders should feel like they have a shot to be division champions. The Commanders are flawed, without question, but sit just two games behind the Giants in the division. It's not like New York is a lock to run away with it.

The biggest problem for the Commanders is the loss of receiver Terry McLaurin for the season. It leaves them thin at receiver, and the good news is there are a lot of veterans available at the deadline at various price points. The Commanders should be interested. They also should be interested in improving a secondary that ranks 27th in passing yards allowed.

The biggest question for the Ravens is this: Can Lamar Jackson return for the playoffs from a thumb injury suffered on Sunday? If the answer is yes, it's not outrageous for a team with a .500 record to see what it can do to keep playoff hopes alive until Jackson can come back. The problem is that it's hard to find any quarterback who can save a season (contrary to everything you see before the trade deadline, NFL teams aren't excited to trade away their backup quarterback). Still, the Ravens have to look. As much as the Ravens like Tyler Huntley, he's not the answer, especially now that he's dealing with a toe injury. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano is very, very unlikely to keep the Ravens in playoff contention.

However, if Jackson is done for the rest of the season with no hope for the playoffs, the Ravens probably have to turn the page and sell. It would hurt, but it would kickstart what could be a huge offseason of change in Baltimore. Because without Jackson, the Ravens' ranking of No. 22 here might be generous.

The Falcons are in a weird space. They're tied with the Buccaneers for second place in the NFC South, a half game behind the Panthers (3-4). They also are one of the most inconsistent teams in the NFL. They followed up beating the previously undefeated 49ers by losing to a Buccaneers team that didn't complete a single pass.

Atlanta is wildly inconsistent on offense, and that's why adding a receiver to go alongside Drake London makes sense. But the offense should be good enough, when it's not playing in a rainstorm like Sunday, to contend in the division. The defense needs help. And it could use it at almost every position aside from off-ball linebacker and safety. It's weird for a 3-5 team to clearly be buyers, but that's the 2026 NFC South.

A sub-.500 team that just fired its defensive coordinator also doesn't profile as a buyer, but the Panthers are in the 2026 NFC South. Their defense needs help, and firing Ejiro Evero doesn't solve all the problems. Being without cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson, who are both on injured reserve, is tough to overcome. Getting some help there would be wise. A pass rusher would be nice too, considering Jaelan Phillips has been injured and isn't living up to his $120 million contract signed in the offseason.

It's not like the offense doesn't need help too, particularly the offensive line's depth because of injuries. Coming off an NFC South title and striving for another, the Panthers will be looking around before the deadline. There are a few areas that could use help.

The Texans made a big and questionable move in the offseason, trading fourth- and seventh-round draft picks, along with offensive lineman Juice Scruggs, to the Lions for running back David Montgomery. Scruggs has been more valuable this season than Montgomery, who has averaged 2.7 yards per carry and missed two games with injury. Woody Marks hasn't been much better. Houston has no running game and it's a big reason it is 2-5.

Do the Texans possibly trade for another running back? Do they trade for anyone at all? It's hard to give up the idea that Houston can still get back in the playoff race. It's a talented but underachieving team. But the Texans still have a 33.8% shot to make the playoffs, via DVOA, and can theoretically be a dangerous playoff opponent. Is that enough to ship off more picks, especially if it's for another running back?

Biggest need: Not being myopic about trading picks

A team two games under .500 now has a 57.4% chance to host a playoff game as a division winner, according to DVOA. The NFC South, everyone!

The Buccaneers might have been sellers two weeks ago, with veterans like receiver Chris Godwin Jr. and defensive end YaYa Diaby available, but that mentality likely changes after decisive wins over the Panthers and Falcons. Still, this is a 3-5 team and advanced metrics say the Bucs are pretty good as is (they rank a surprising fifth in DVOA). Tampa doesn't have a pressing need, though defensive help is always welcomed. The Buccaneers can stand pat, keep their picks and still be the favorite in the NFC South while not giving away any valuable picks for the future.

Biggest need: Remembering the long-term plan

It's hard for a franchise that hasn't had much success over the past few decades to have a level head over a solid start to the season. At 4-4, the Raiders can talk themselves into being playoff contenders. That makes it hard to be a seller. It would be an even harder thing to explain to longtime fans who are dying for a taste of success or a new fan base in Las Vegas that hasn't fully embraced the Raiders yet.

Realistically, the Raiders probably should be closer to sellers than they are to buyers. Could they find out if a team is willing to pay a heavy premium for Maxx Crosby like the Ravens (almost) did in March? It's not like the Ravens' concerns about Crosby's knee over the long term have vanished. However, ESPN reported the Raiders have no plans to trade Crosby. It also seems very unlikely the Raiders trade Kirk Cousins, but what if a desperate team is willing to overpay for a viable quarterback who already has 19 touchdown passes? Wouldn't they have to listen? It's not like Cousins is the future and they'll want to get Fernando Mendoza some valuable reps before the end of the season even if Cousins stays aboard. It seems foolish to be buyers when they're well behind the Broncos and Chiefs in the AFC West. And the big picture says that they should be quietly gauging the market on Crosby, Cousins and any others without long-term value, even if that would be unpopular to many Raiders fans.

Like the Raiders, it's fun for a team that has had almost no success to start 5-2. An uncompetitive loss to the Steelers on Sunday should put the Browns in a more realistic mindset. They can't keep living off last-minute wins, and their poor quarterback situation makes their level of success unsustainable. The five wins have already put the Browns in a bad spot to find a quarterback solution in 2027, but that's a conversation for next offseason.

The Browns can still be partial sellers without hurting their playoff hopes for this season. Receiver Jerry Jeudy is tradable and there are plenty of teams that could use him. Offensive tackle Dawand Jones, a backup who could provide depth elsewhere, can also be available. But with a promising young core, the Browns have to be careful to not get ahead of themselves despite a 5-3 record.

The Giants landing a running back is one of the easiest predictions of the trade deadline. They have plenty of injuries at the position, seem lukewarm at best on Cam Skattebo, but have a great chance to win a bad division.

How much do the Giants want to pay for a running back? Jonathan Taylor is the dream, but he won't be cheap. Perhaps Tony Pollard will be more reasonable, though he has played very well lately and that could increase the price.

The Giants will be looking at every possibility to help at running back, which could push them closer to a division title.

The Packers are one of a few teams in need of a running back and it's a different situation than the rest. If Josh Jacobs was a sure thing the rest of the season, the Packers might concentrate on more offensive line help or simply hold tight, knowing Micah Parsons is on the way soon.

But Jacobs' legal situation took a turn over the weekend after more allegations of abuse were reported. He denied wrongdoing, but the NFL can revisit the case. We have seen how poor the Packers' running game was without Jacobs. Green Bay doesn't want to be stuck again in that situation if Jacobs faces further punishment. Adding a viable starter would allow the Packers to move on from Jacobs entirely.

Biggest need: Receiver or cornerback, but probably nothing

A team that has among the oldest rosters in the NFL and is 6-2 before the deadline might generally be a big buyer to make a push with an aging team. Yet, it doesn't seem like there's one move that can put the Steelers on the same level as some of the NFL's elite teams.

Another receiver would be nice, but there's a lot of money tied up in DK Metcalf, and someone like Josh Downs would be redundant with the skill set of intriguing rookie Germie Bernard. Perhaps adding Jacksonville's Brian Thomas Jr. would make sense. Cornerback could help after trading away Joey Porter Jr., but the Steelers have been good at that position without him. An old team trading away valuable picks seems bad for the future. And a 6-2 team trading someone like edge rusher Alex Highsmith seems like the wrong move too. We might see Pittsburgh make a minor move or two but little else.

The Rams have already invested heavily into the 2026 roster, so what's the big deal in sending off more draft picks? For now, the Rams are playing coy, saying that players they could get back from injury, like Myles Garrett and Davante Adams, would serve as their deadline additions.

"Based on our situation, I mean the good thing for us is, what you look at is hopefully some of those trades will be guys getting back from injury that haven't played for us," head coach Sean McVay said, via the Los Angeles Times. "That's kind of the way we look at it."

Yet, it's hard to believe that because of the Rams' history. And while the idea of getting Adams back from a major hamstring injury is good in theory, he'll turn 34 on Dec. 24 and it's not a guarantee he returns to his normal level. The Rams are very thin at receiver behind Puka Nacua while Adams heals, and it's not like Nacua doesn't have a long injury history. Maybe the Rams stay put, but it wouldn't be a surprise if they talk themselves into a deal. Grabbing an exciting receiver might give the sluggish Rams a spark.

The Dolphins don't have a good pass rush but they still pressured Drake Maye often in Week 8. Maye overcame that with a strong second half to lead the Patriots to a win, but it's not like the line issues are going away. Guards Mike Onwenu and Alijah Vera-Tucker are on injured reserve. Getting a guard to help makes a lot of sense.

The Patriots have also had some trade speculation on the selling side. Cornerback Carlton Davis III could be dealt, according to Albert Breer of SI.com. Davis returned from a neck injury for Week 8 and played 96.9% of the defensive snaps, but it's possible the Patriots want to trade him for extra draft capital, which they could use to improve at guard.

Biggest need: Some help for Jaxon Smith-Njigba

It's surprising to see Smith-Njigba at a 36.3% target share entering Monday night's game, because it's rare for a receiver to get that many of a team's targets. But then you look around Seattle's offense and realize there's no other viable option. Smith-Njigba has 985 yards this season and Cooper Kupp is second on the team at 206.

The Seahawks decided to address their run game by adding guard Quenton Nelson instead of one of the name-brand running backs who might be available. Maybe that's their only big move. But for an offense that has been uneven most of the season, another receiving threat would help. It would help take pressure off turnover-prone Sam Darnold.

The idea that the Broncos could make a big move for Jonathan Taylor is dubious only because Sean Payton's history of using committees at running back without a standout workhorse. And the team has to be intrigued by rookie Jonah Coleman, who has played well and came up with two big plays to give Denver the lead in a huge win over the Chiefs on Sunday.

Perhaps Taylor or another big-time back could solve some issues on the offense. Or maybe it's a receiver or a tight end, after the Evan Engram signing in 2025 has been a dud. Even some depth on the offensive line isn't a bad idea. The Broncos are set on defense, so their focus can be how to add an impact piece to an inconsistent offense.

Biggest need: Defense, particularly at cornerback

The Lions' fan base wasn't happy when the Cowboys overpaid to get cornerback Joey Porter Jr. in a trade. They know that cornerback is an issue and it seems hard to believe the deadline will pass without Detroit doing something at the position.

Yet, there are other issues on a defense that has struggled most of the season, though it has allowed just 32 points the last two games. While the human element of linebacker Jack Campbell's neck injury is overwhelming, and his recovery is the biggest part of that story, there is a football side to it as well. Detroit will presumably be without one of the best off-ball linebackers in the NFL indefinitely. While the team's thoughts are primarily on their young star's health, the Lions also have to deal with the reality of perhaps adding a linebacker before the deadline.

Biggest need: Receiver, but don't forget about offensive line

This is no surprise: The Chiefs still need help at receiver. Their offense has been built around Kenneth Walker III to good results, but it's an incomplete unit. Rashee Rice is productive but not a dominant No. 1, Xavier Worthy hasn't broken out and there's not much else to speak of. Among the Chiefs' wideouts, Rice has 243 yards, Worthy has 230, Tyquan Thornton has 219 but he's on injured reserve and nobody else has more than 65. It's a team that is a perfect candidate to try to turn around Brian Thomas Jr.'s career.

But the Chiefs also can't ignore the offensive line. Guard Kingsley Suamataia was benched for the second time this season on Sunday. Offensive tackle Josh Simmons has been a problem and was put on IR. Receiver would be the more splashy move, but adding to the offensive line might be even more prudent.

Biggest need: Interior offensive line, and maybe Jonathan Taylor too

Trading for Jonathan Taylor, which has been rumored, would be a big headline in Minnesota before the trade deadline. Taylor would obviously help, but it's not like there aren't other issues on the offense. Quarterback might be one of them but Minnesota isn't going to make a difference-making move there.

The Vikings could add Taylor and still have trouble blocking for him. They're thin at guard after Donovan Jackson suffered a torn meniscus in Week 4. Their starting guards on Sunday, Joe Huber and Will Fries, rank 33rd and 41st among guards in Pro Football Focus' grades. But, an upgrade like Taylor could make everyone look better. It would be a fun trade for everyone.

Biggest need: More defensive help, this time on the back end

The Bengals got the win in overtime Sunday and a bump up in the rankings, but there were some troubling signs. Tennessee's offense was one of the worst in the NFL and it gained 440 yards and scored 36 points on the Bengals. Given Cincinnati's defensive issues in recent seasons, it was worrisome even in the win.

"I know we have the guys in there that are happy we won, but they're not satisfied with our overall performance," Bengals head coach Zac Taylor said, via the team's transcripts. "Each position group will go through that and find things we have to be better at."

The Bengals' line has been better with additions Dexter Lawrence II and Boye Mafe (Lawrence came up with huge plays in the win over the Titans), but the back seven could use some work. Help at cornerback or safety would be nice, and while the Bengals are trying to see it through with young linebackers Barrett Carter and Demetrius Knight Jr., they could use an upgrade there too. Cincinnati is a respectable 15th in defensive DVOA, but the difference between it making a deep playoff run or losing early on could be a defensive addition at the deadline.

Biggest need: Still defense, though the big move was made

The Bears' front office understood the assignment. Chicago traded two first-round draft picks to Tennessee for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. If there's a bigger move at the deadline from any team, it'll be a surprise. Simmons is exactly what the Bears' defense needed as a disruptor on the line, and he notched a sack in his Chicago debut on Monday night against Seattle. Chicago clearly feels like it's a contender now and was willing to sacrifice some high future draft picks for a shot at making a deep playoff run.

That doesn't mean the Bears should be done on defense, though any other move wouldn't be major. A mid-round draft pick for pass rushing help would continue to improve the defensive front. A reunion with Khalil Mack would make a ton of sense. But make no mistake: The Bears already made their all-in move.

"Super Bowl teams all have what we call a 'red-level' interior defensive lineman," Bears general manager Ryan Poles said of the Simmons trade, via the Chicago Sun-Times. "You need one.

"We've been searching, but sometimes the draft doesn't provide that to you. Free agency doesn't really [provide them]; it's very hard for guys to get out of the building when they have all of those things that we're talking about. [Simmons] was an opportunity that we had to jump on."

Biggest need: Offensive and defensive line help

The aggressive mindset that general manager James Gladstone wants to be known for will be put to the test. The Jaguars are one of the best teams in the NFL. Jacksonville has also dealt with two major injuries that need to be addressed.

Left tackle Anton Harrison tore his ACL in Week 5. Then defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton, who had been playing very well against the run this season, tore his quad Sunday and is done for the season. Walker Little has done a good job replacing Harrison, and perhaps that leads Jacksonville to look for offensive line depth rather than an impact starter. Replacing Hamilton with a high-end defensive tackle would be a strong move. Grover Stewart of Indianapolis might be a possibility, though the Colts might not want to trade within the division. If the Eagles trade defensive tackle Moro Ojomo, he could make a difference. It's time to see how aggressive Gladstone plans to be now that Jacksonville has one of the best teams in the NFL.

For once, finding weapons around Josh Allen isn't the top priority for the Bills. That has shifted to the defense. That group looked fine on Sunday, but that's because Lamar Jackson was knocked out after one play. Buffalo looked good against Baltimore's second and third quarterbacks, but the rest of the season has been rough. The Bills are 24th in yards and points allowed, and that's with an easy day against the Ravens included. Baltimore had 144 yards; Buffalo has given up at least 348 in every other game.

The Bills don't have the salary cap space to make a huge move on defense, but they should be looking into help at all three levels, with an emphasis on the back end. Only two teams are giving up more passing yards per game. Even if it's a mid-level move at cornerback or safety, the Bills know what they have to do. The Super Bowl window is wide open if the defense is good enough.

Biggest need: DeForest Buckner fills it, though maybe other moves are possible

The 49ers made a smart move to bring back DeForest Buckner in a trade with the Colts. Buckner might not be at his peak, like he was with his first go-around with the 49ers, but he's still a very good defensive lineman. The 49ers needed that. They also are hoping to get Nick Bosa back after the bye, which would be a big boost.

San Francisco has to weigh making improvements now for a team that has dealt with many injuries, particularly at receiver, vs. restocking with draft picks. The 49ers haven't drafted well in recent years and that has hurt their depth. That hasn't been a problem this season but it's looming. San Francisco also understands how a huge move can have a wide-ranging effect: A massive trade during the 2022 season for Christian McCaffrey boosted the team to a Super Bowl a season later and is still paying off. A trade for a receiver or defensive help would strengthen the 49ers' standing as the Super Bowl favorite, but they have to keep an eye on the future as well.

#2742. Every Man United player to also play for Aston Villa

Manchester United will welcome Aston Villa to Old Trafford on Sunday.

The two sides have seen numerous players represent both clubs over the years, particularly in recent seasons.

Here is a list of the players with the most appearances for United who have also represented the Villans.

The United academy product has played over 400 times for the Red Devils but spent the second half of the 2025 season on loan at Villa.

He impressed most in the Champions League quarter-final defeat to Paris Saint-Germain and secured a loan move to FC Barcelona the following season on the back of his fine displays at Villa Park.

The Great Dane's final act as a Manchester United player was to captain the side to the treble in 1999. He then left for Sporting CP in Portugal but rejoined the Premier League in 2001.

He spent one season at Villa Park, playing 36 games, but also managed to score one goal.

Lindelof spent eight seasons at Old Trafford, leaving in 2025.

The Swede joined Villa that summer and helped secure the Europa League victory last year, playing a key part in their season.

Young spent four seasons at Villa before he was transferred to United in 2011.

The winger would spend nine seasons at Old Trafford and would captain the side later in his career.

The Irish centre-back was a mainstay of the United defence in the 1980s but joined Villa in 1989.

He spent seven years in Birmingham before leaving for Derby County in 1996.

Wan-Bissaka spent five seasons at Old Trafford after signing in 2019.

The Congolese defender joined West Ham United that summer, but after the Hammers were relegated last season, he joined Villa on loan.

Chicago got things started early, silencing the crowd at Lumen Field with a methodical, 17-play opening drive that ended in Williams finding Luther Burden III in the end zone on a 1-yard touchdown pass.

#2736. Bears v. Seahawks Postgame: A Statement Victory in Big Jeff’s First Game

Chicago opened with a grinding 17-play, 80-yard drive that consumed 8 minutes and 32 seconds and ended with Caleb Williams' 1-yard touchdown pass to Luther Burden. It was the first time in 27 games that an opponent had scored on the Seahawks on the opening possession. Jeffery Simmons made an immediate impact in his Bears debut with a sack of Sam Darnold.

Observation: The Bears set the tone early by sustaining drives and staying physical against a defense that had been difficult to score on.Gooch Hot Take: That opening drive wasn't flashy—it was the kind of ugly, clock-eating football that tells a contender "we can hang with you for four quarters." Simmons already looks like the interior disruptor the Bears paid two firsts for. But let's be clear – that first touchdown drive was EVERYTHING the Bears want to be.

Seattle got on the board with a Jason Myers field goal. Chicago answered with Cairo Santos field goals from 44 and 38 yards to push the lead to 13-3. With 30 seconds left, Jaxon Smith-Njigba beat coverage for a 43-yard touchdown from Darnold (extra point missed), cutting the deficit to 13-9 at the half.

Observation: The Bears were efficient enough in the red zone area to take points when available. JSN remains the one consistent explosive piece for Seattle.

Upon Further Review preview: We're going to talk about the QB slide this week. Nothing Bush could do – literally flying through the air with his back turned – on that late Darnold slide. The TV crew thought it was a clear penalty – and maybe it was on the rules – the rules need to change. It's just ridiculous – and it isn't protecting quarterbacks.

It isn't even that it produces dumb penalties – because of course you cannot ask defenders to stop in midair. It is the fact that it encourages QBs to slide – which is an uber-dangerous play for them. When QBs become runners – they should just be runners.

Gooch Hot Take: Santos quietly outkicked Myers when it mattered. The Seattle punter kind of rocks – respect given. But the other Hawks kicker – the missed extra point on the JSN score was the difference between a one-score game and a more comfortable margin heading into the locker room.

That opening 17-play drive was the statement of the half. It wasn't explosive, but it was the kind of grinding, clock-eating football that shows Chicago can match Seattle's physicality for a full game.

Simmons is already justifying the early returns on the trade. One sack and consistent pressure in his first half as a Bear is exactly the multiplier the defensive line needed.

JSN remains Seattle's entire explosive element. When he's bottled up, the rest of the offense looks ordinary. The missed extra point on his score was a quiet but meaningful swing.

Santos is quietly having a strong night. Two clean field goals kept the Bears in control when the red-zone finishing wasn't perfect.

If Chicago continues to control the line of scrimmage and limit big plays outside of JSN, this is a very manageable second half. Seattle will need more than one or two explosive plays to flip the script on the road.

The Bears REALLY need to solve the final drive of the half. This is the second week in a row they've allowed a soft touchdown heading into halftime.

Chicago answered the half-ending JSN score by controlling the third period and pushing the lead to two possessions. The Seahawks were held scoreless as the Bears continued to win the physical battle and sustain drives.

The Bears opened the half with the ball and marched 69 yards in 10 plays over 6 minutes and 19 seconds. The drive featured a 22-yard completion from Caleb Williams to Rome Odunze and a 9-yard pass to Kalif Raymond that set up short-yardage situations. D'Andre Swift finished it with a 1-yard touchdown run, and Cairo Santos' extra point made it 20-9.

Seattle's best chance late in the quarter was erased by offensive pass interference on Jaxon Smith-Njigba, wiping out a gain that would have put them near the goal line and leaving them with second-and-long instead.

Chicago's second drive of six-plus minutes ended in a touchdown, matching the pattern from the opening series. They are controlling the clock and the line of scrimmage against a Seahawks defense that has been hard to move.

Williams continues to deliver timely completions under pressure. The connection to Odunze on the drive was another example of him extending plays and finding open receivers.

Seattle's offense remains limited outside of isolated JSN moments. The OPI call was a tough break, but the Bears' defense is generating pressure and forcing incomplete or short gains.

Jeffery Simmons continues to show up as a disruptor in his debut, contributing to the interior pressure that has helped limit Darnold.

Swift's short-yardage score perfectly complemented the long opening drive. Chicago is winning with sustained, physical football rather than relying on explosives, and that is the harder style for Seattle to counter.

The OPI wipeout of JSN's potential scoring chance was a quiet but significant swing. Seattle is not generating enough consistent offense to overcome those kinds of setbacks right now. I thought it was the right call – JSN clearly pushed off. The only surprise is that the refs actually called it.

If the Bears keep stacking six-minute drives and finishing them in the end zone, this game is going to get out of reach even if JSN makes another big play. The Seahawks need a quick answer early in the fourth or the physical edge Chicago has established will decide the night.

The final period featured the night's most debated moments and Seattle's closest push. Early in the quarter, Austin Booker blocked a Jason Myers field-goal attempt, preserving Chicago's two-score lead. On the ensuing possession, Colston Loveland caught a short pass, then fumbled after a hit from DeMarcus Lawrence, who recovered at the Chicago 25. Seattle converted the turnover with a 7-yard touchdown pass from Darnold to Cooper Kupp and a successful two-point conversion to Tory Horton, cutting the lead to 20-17.

Chicago answered with two more Swift rushing touchdowns (5 yards each), the second set up in part by a Kalif Raymond screen, to push the final margin to 34-17. A late interception sealed the outcome.

The late-third-quarter OPI on JSN that wiped out a near-goal-line opportunity remained a point of contention. It was the kind of contact that draws flags inconsistently depending on the crew and the moment.

The Loveland fumble was forced cleanly by Lawrence, but the timing—right after the blocked kick—flipped field position and briefly brought Seattle back within one score.

Earlier in the game, a potential late hit on Darnold by Devin Bush drew criticism as a no-call; the broadcast and social reaction suggested it met the criteria for unnecessary roughness on a sliding quarterback, though no flag was thrown. I don't agree; even if it is technically a foul, we need to get the game back to reflecting real football.

Delay-of-game timing on Chicago snaps and a post-play flag that forced a replay of a down also drew complaints about consistency.

Even with the turnover and the OPI debate, Chicago's response was decisive. Swift's three rushing touchdowns closed the game after Seattle got within three.

Simmons' early sack and continued interior presence set a defensive tone that limited Seattle outside of the one JSN score and the short Kupp touchdown.

The blocked field goal and the subsequent fumble were the swing plays of the fourth. Seattle capitalized on the turnover, but Chicago's ability to answer immediately with sustained scoring drives showed the difference in control.

This was the most complete performance of the season so far from Chicago. They won the physical battle against the team that had been the gold standard on that side of the ball.

Final takeaway: Chicago didn't just survive Seattle. They out-physicaled them, controlled the tempo, weathered the controversial moments and the one turnover, and let Swift finish the job. That's the profile of a team that expects to be playing in January.

The Dallas Mavericks dropped an ugly, grueling game to the Sacramento Kings by a score of 115-110. It was the kind of performance that makes you wonder why any of us spend any time watching sports at all. Dallas, fresh off their most emotional win of the season, laid a massive egg on their home floor and made the winless Kings look like the Harlem Globetrotters.

Dallas shot 7-of-33 from behind the line while Sacramento went 19—of-43. In the modern NBA, you're not going to win any games when the other team outscores you by 36 from three. #2730. 'The one thing they lack': Shane Bond shares honest opinion on India's bowling attack

'The one thing they lack': Shane Bond shares honest opinion on India's bowling attack originally appeared on Cricket News. Add Cricket News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Shane Bond praises India's pace depth but identifies the lack of a left-arm fast bowler.

The former New Zealand pacer backs Siraj and the potential of Aquib Nabi and Akash Deep.

Bond says Gambhir has enough pace options to rotate bowlers and manage workloads.

Ex-New Zealand fast bowler Shane Bond has complimented the bowling assets of India's pace attack but feels the country will do well by having a left-arm fast bowler before the 2027 ODI World Cup.

In an interview with Times of India, he spoke about how India has everything in terms of pace, height and skills.

"The one thing they perhaps lack is a left-arm fast bowler, but they've got height, pace and skill. They hit the seam hard and, importantly, they have depth," Bond opined.

Considering that the 2027 World Cup is due to be hosted by South Africa, variety in the pace attack might come in handy.

MORE:Bond defends Bumrah's decision to prioritise Tests over ODIs vs NZ

Bond has found much admiration in Mohammed Siraj, who has developed into one of the most dependable fast bowling options for India.

"I'm a huge fan of Mohammed Siraj. I love his energy and body language. He's been performing consistently across formats for a long time," Bond commented.

Siraj is anticipated to lead India's pace attack in the upcoming ODI series against New Zealand as Jasprit Bumrah and Hardik Pandya have been ruled out.

Bond also praised the rise of Auqib Nabi, who has shone in domestic cricket with some remarkable performances, while complimenting Akash Deep.

"Even someone like Auqib Nabi has come through and looks like a quality bowler. Akash Deep is a good bowler too," he concluded.

MORE:Pandya's next IPL team: Franchises in talks with MI over possible trade

Though recognising the deficiency of a left-handed fast bowler as a potential flaw, Bond feels India have sufficient calibre players to enable rotation among the pace attack.

"As a coach, Gautam Gambhir will want enough options to rest and rotate players, and India certainly have that luxury," he remarked.

Rotation of workload is becoming very crucial now, with fast bowlers having to juggle both international cricket and franchise commitments. Bumrah's exclusion from the ODI series against New Zealand ahead of the upcoming Test series is one such instance.

According to Bond, India's strength in their bowling ranks will help them keep their fast bowlers fit and fresh for major tournaments.

MORE:India and Pakistan could face each other upto 10 times in the upcoming year

Bond's analysis is a reminder of the fact that India possesses excellent depth when it comes to fast bowlers; however, having various bowling options is equally important as having quality ones.

Having a left-arm pacer can certainly give India another weapon in their arsenal, especially away from home. Even though Arshdeep Singh is a left-arm pacer for India, he lacks experience in ODIs as compared to some other players in the squad.

The arrival of Auqib Nabi and Akash Deep is indeed a welcome development, but Siraj offers some experience and solidity. The challenge for India will lie in converting their strength into a well-balanced attack.

#2729. What's next for Connor Bedard, Blackhawks after massive five-year, $75 million contract extension

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Chicago Blackhawks have locked in their franchise cornerstone for the near future. On Saturday, the Blackhawks announced that star center Connor Bedard has signed a five-year contract worth $75 million.

Bedard's $15 million average annual value makes him the third-highest paid player in the NHL for the 2026-27 season. Only Minnesota Wild winger Kirill Kaprizov ($17 million) and the newly-signed Anaheim Ducks center Leo Carlsson ($18 million) are ahead of him.

"Connor has continuously defied our expectations since being drafted, and has quickly established himself as an elite player in the NHL," Blackhawks general manager Kyle Davidson said in a statement. "He utilizes all aspects of his game to not only be a constant threat, but to make the players around him better every time he steps on the ice. Connor's strong work ethic and determination to always improve his game has set an extraordinary standard for our young core, and we're excited for the incredible impact he'll have in this next chapter of Blackhawks hockey."

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2023 NHL Draft, Bedard has already displayed elite offensive upside, even if his overall game still has work to do. Last season, Bedard posted a career high 75 points in 69 games. In 219 NHL games, Bedard has totaled 75 goals and 128 assists.

The biggest issues for Bedard are durability concerns -- he's played fewer than 70 games in two of three seasons and will miss the first month of the upcoming season with a shoulder injury -- and subpar defense. The defense is a common problem for young centers and should improve in the coming years, but Bedard has now suffered multiple shoulder injuries in his career.

With Bedard's long-term contract finalized, both he and the Blackhawks will try to take the next step toward greatness. For the player, that means refining his game in order to become the $15 million man most believe him to be. For the team, that means surrounding Bedard with an adequate supporting cast for the first time in his career.

First and foremost, Bedard needs to get healthy and stay healthy. After missing 13 games with a shoulder injury last year, Bedard suffered another injury that required surgery to fix, and he will miss roughly a dozen games out of the gate in 2026-27. Those issues may delay his jump into the NHL's elite tier of players.

Once back at full strength, Bedard will have to show improvement defensively. He oozes offensive ability, but if Bedard is going to be a true No. 1 franchise center, he has to thrive at both ends of the ice. With Bedard on the ice at five-on-five last season, Chicago surrendered 3.60 xGA/60, per Natural Stat Trick. That was the second-worst number on the team with rookie Anton Frondell bringing up the rear.

That doesn't necessarily mean Bedard was the Blackhawks' worst defensive player, but it does mean he often struggled when going up against the opposing team's best players. Stars -- especially those raking in $15 million per season -- are expected to drive play for their team regardless of circumstance. Bedard didn't do that last season.

Bedard also needs to show more growth in the face-off circle. To his credit, Bedard has already done that, going from 38.9% as a rookie to 47.1% last season. Still, Chicago would probably like to see Bedard closer to 50%, especially with him taking key draws in big moments. Maybe that number keeps rising as Bedard gets strong and adds more tricks in the dot.

If Bedard can round out his game without the puck, $15 million per season will be a very fair deal, especially as salaries explode across the league.

We've already seen what can happen when a restricted free agent has all the leverage in contract negotiations. The Ducks were essentially backed into a $90 million contract after the Philadelphia Flyers signed Carlsson to a massive offer sheet.

That risk was there for Bedard too, which is why Davidson deserves some credit for signing him at a more reasonable cap hit. Bedard still has work to do in order to reach that price point, but his ceiling is worth at least $15 million per season.

The Blackhawks can help their young star by putting more NHL-caliber players around him. Chicago tore it down to the studs in hopes of landing Bedard in the 2023 draft, and while that plan worked, it also created a roster full of holes around the No. 1overall pick. Over the last three seasons, Bedard has had little help.

Chicago already improved its defense this offseason when it acquired Bowen Byram from the Buffalo Sabres. Say what you will about the acquisition cost or his $75 contract extension, but Byram inarguably makes Chicago better on the blue line. That unit still needs work, but it's a step in the right direction.

The real issue is finding Bedard a quality running mate at the top of the lineup. Outside of Bedard, only one other player topped 50 points in 2025-26, and it was 31-year-old Tyler Bertuzzi. Chicago still has $14.1 million in cap space with which to add some firepower, but some upgrades will have to come internally.

It's conceivable that the Blackhawks' lineup will include seven players selected inside the top 50 picks of the last five drafts.

That's an exciting proposition, and fans have reasons to be optimistic about the future. That said, none of those players have really established themselves as future stars, outside of Bedard. Frondell, Nazar and Rinzel seem like the best bets to get there soon, but that's based more on projection than anything tangible.

The first month of the season should be an excellent barometer for the Blackhawks as they assess those players. Bedard will be out of the lineup, and it'll be interesting to see who sinks and who swims until he returns. Once Chicago establishes exactly what it has in its young nucleus, Davidson can then go out and aggressively address needs via trades and free agency.

#2728. Warriors' Draymond Green ejected after shove match with Dillon Brooks

SAN FRANCISCO ― There's no love lost between Golden State Warriors forward Draymond Green and Phoenix Suns guard Dillon Brooks.

The two have a history of trash-talking and getting into shoving matches with one another. They kept that tension going during the Warriors-Suns matchup on Monday, Nov. 2.

Green committed a foul against Suns center Khaman Maluach, wrapping him up in an intentional foul before throwing him to the ground. Green was initially called for a foul and then an ensuing technical foul for shoving Maluach to the ground.

Things got spicy and Green got a visit from his old friend, or foe, Brooks. Brooks took exception to Green's push on his teammate and ran to the pile, pushing Green.

Green retaliated as teammates, coaches and game officials had to separate the two players. Both Green and Brooks received double-technical fouls for the dust up.

It was Green's second technical, which resulted in an automatic disqualification. Green left the game at the 10-minute mark of the third quarter. He finished the game with four points, four rebounds, two assists and a steal in 17 minutes.

The Warriors went on to win the game, 116-113.

The Warriors were receptive to Green's ejection. It lit a fire under the team, teammate Stephen Curry said.

"We had to respond so I'm glad we did," Curry said. "It was a combination of that moment. We're going to have out brother's back when he defends us."

Head coach Steve Kerr said he doesn't want actual fights, but rather the team's competitive nature.

"I just want to see the competitive spirit, and I thought we saw that time," Kerr said. "They really punched us in the mouth. You know, that first quarter, they were ready. ... I was thrilled with our competitive spirit. And I know there were a couple dust-ups, but that's just, you know, the greatest NBA basketball players on Earth competing. This is what it is."

Warriors guard Brandin Podziemski said he loved Green's intensity.

"We didn't have the edge to us to start the game," Podziemski said. "Found it a little bit in the second quarter but then they came out in the third quarter pretty well and that kind of changed the game for us. Everybody's locked and came together for Dray. So I think it was needed."

#2727. Seahawks vs. Bears post-game reaction: What we learned from a damaging Monday night defeat

The Seattle Seahawks are in trouble. By no means is the season over at 4-4, but the NFC is deep enough just through the North alone that Seattle has to worry about making the playoffs, forget about making it back to the top of the NFC West. Their 34-17 loss to the Chicago Bears was their heaviest under Mike Macdonald since 2024, and the defense finally broke down after the offense spent the whole night spamming three-and-outs.

Myself and Bryce Coutts are here for post-game immediate reaction podcast, which will start at around 8:40 pm PT. You can catch it live or just watch it afterward when you're in a mood to listen to a lot of ranting.

Brian Fleury's magic lasted a week, he's back on the hot seat. Where was the sense of urgency in this offense? Why are they constantly burning early downs with runs to the weaker side of the offensive line? Why does the offense look so consistently labored? How is the offense this broken when the ball isn't being thrown to JSN? Fleury looks like he's not in a good position to lead this offense.

Sam Darnold was terrible and worse than the stats suggested. The one pick was kind to Darnold. The sack number could've been much higher if not for repeated undisciplined penalties by the Bears secondary. He had happy feet, inaccurate throws, basically everything we weren't seeing last week against the Kansas City Chiefs. This is not a quarterback playing with confidence or trusting what he sees, and the combo of his struggles and Fleury's struggles could be tied together.

It turns out the running game just isn't magically fixed overnight. Quenton Nelson is here, which is cool. Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price are back. That's super cool. The run game stinks. That's not cool. Only 61 yards on 17 carries from running backs.

Even "The Dark Side" is fallible. Caleb Williams made some magnificent plays, but the Seahawks defense was not at their sharpest. They gave up a few preventable pass game explosives, and that screen to Kalif Raymond at 20-17 was a killer to concede. With Leonard Williams out with a stinger, the hope is it's not a major issue because the d-line gets much thinner when he's not in the lineup, and the defense is worse off. Nick Emmanwori was last week's darling and one of this week's worst performers.

The Seahawks special teams was horrendous. Penalties, missed kicks, blocked field goals, and poor kick returns galore. This was an unacceptable performance by a unit that was magnificent last year and has been way too inconsistent this year.

Seattle's postseason hopes are in jeopardy. While Seattle doesn't have another daunting stretch on the schedule, this team isn't playing well enough to trust that they're capable of comfortably winning against anyone right now. A lot of things need fixing and I'm not sure how much can be fixed this year.

#2726. Jets star goalie Connor Hellebuyck requests trade: Where three-time Vezina Trophy winner could land

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After months of speculation about his future in Winnipeg, Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck has confirmed his trade request publicly.

Hellebuyck's name has come up in trade rumors since the 2025-26 season ended, and the rumor mill will only pick back up now that he's gone public with his request. NHL training camps will open soon, and Hellebuyck wanted to provide more clarity on the situation.

"Winnipeg has been home for my entire NHL career, and I will always be grateful for my time there.

"I have never forgotten June 23, 2012. That's the day Winnipeg took a chance on a goalie playing in Odessa, Texas. I gave everything I had from that moment to prove the Jets made the right decision.

"Several months ago, I privately requested a trade. I have tried to handle the situation quietly and respectfully while giving the organization time to explore its options.

"With training camp approaching, I felt it was important to publicly confirm my request. My position has not changed, and I believe moving on is the best path forward for me and my family.

"I appreciate everything Winnipeg Jets fans have meant to me throughout my career and hope a resolution can be reached soon."

In what would become one of the biggest steals in NHL Draft history, the Jets used the No. 130 overall pick to select Hellebucyk in 2012. Just seven years later, Hellebuyck established himself as one of the best goalies in the lea, and he's maintained that level of play for nearly a decade.

A three-time Vezina Trophy winner, Hellebuyck has a legitimate claim as the best goaltender in the world. Over the last three seasons, Hellebucyk has totaled 73.4 goals saved above average, per Natural Stat Trick. That's 20 more than the next closest goaltender -- Andrei Vasilevskiy -- and includes a rather underwhelming 2025-26 campaign.

There have been plenty of years in which Hellebuyck carried mediocre Jets teams, but 2025-26 was not one of them. He actually allowed 0.35 goals above average with a pedestrian 0.895 save percentage. Normally, it would be fair to worry about a 33-year-old goalie with those numbers, but not in Hellebucyk's case.

Hellebuyck backstopped Team USA to its first men's ice hockey gold medal in 46 years at the 2026 Olympics while allowing a total of six goals and boasting a .956 save percentage. He was exceptional in the final against Canada, where he turned away 41 of the 42 shots he faced and made one of the most iconic saves in hockey history.

THAT WAS ONE HELLE-BUYCK OF A STOP. 😳 pic.twitter.com/N3wCimdBGw

The biggest obstacle in a trade might be Hellebucyk's contract. He has five years remaining on his current deal at $8.5 million per season -- and while that may be a lot of term for a goalie his age -- Hellebucyk is worth a lot more than that at his best. The real issue is that he owns a full no-movement clause, which means Hellebuyck controls his fate, and the trade request going public certainly won't improve the team's leverage.

So, where does Hellebucyk land? Without knowing his preferred destinations, it's probably safe to assume that he wants the opportunity to win a Stanley Cup, and the team that acquires him will need the requisite cap space and resources to do so.

With those parameters in mind, here are five teams that could make sense as Hellebuyck trade suitors.

The Sabres were one of two teams frequently connected to Hellebuyck earlier in the offseason, and that makes sense. Buffalo is an ascending team with room to upgrade in the crease. Not to denigrate Alex Lyon and Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen, who were a formidable tandem in 2025-26, but I'm not sure Buffalo can bet on similar performances this upcoming season. Adding Hellebuyck would eliminate that question mark immediately and make the Sabres a favorite to win the Atlantic Division.

In fact, one of Luukkonen or Lyon could go back to Winnipeg to help provide stability in the post-Hellebuyck era. The Sabres also own all their first-round picks for the foreseeable future, and it would probably take at least two of those to pry Hellebuyck from the Jets. Just a year ago, it would be hard to believe that Hellebuyck would waive his no-movement clause to go to Buffalo, but it seems very plausible now.

When the Devils traded Jacob Markstrom to the Florida Panthers in July, I assumed it would only be a matter of time until Hellebuyck was in Newark. To this point, nothing has come to fruition, but New Jersey absolutely needs an NHL-caliber starter. Jake Allen, David Rittich and Nico Daws are on the roster right now, and that won't get the job done.

The Devils were undone by poor goaltending -- and subpar defense -- too much last year. Markstrom allowed 13.7 goals above average, per Natural Stat Trick, and even a diminished version of Hellebuyck would provide a significant upgrade over those numbers. New Jersey has the draft capital to get something done, but it also needs to clear cap space, possibly with a Dougie Hamilton salary dump.

They just won the Stanley Cup with Brandon Bussi in net, so the Hurricanes have proven they don't need elite goaltending to go all the way. Regardless, running it back with Bussi wouldn't be a very safe bet, and adding Hellebuyck would only reinforce Carolina's biggest strength. As we saw in the playoffs, the Hurricanes are already one of the best defensive teams in the league. Put Hellebuyck behind that lineup, and scoring on Carolina becomes a Herculean task.

Thanks to savvy cap management by GM Eric Tulsky, Carolina has the room to add Hellebuyck without jettisoning a current player. Oh, and Carolina has three first-round picks over the next two years. If Tulsky wants to pursue Hellebuyck, he has the resources to do it.

This is more of a longshot, but it would be fun to see the Sharks take a swing if this, assuming Hellebuyck would sign off on a trade to San Jose. Despite the fact that they overpaid for it, the Sharks blue line is better, and there is a wealth of young talent at forward. Another factor here is the current state of the Pacific Division, which is abhorrent. The third playoff spot is up for grabs, and the Sharks could secure it with Hellebuyck in goal.

Superstar Macklin Celebrini is on the final year of his entry-level deal before his $18.8 million salary kicks in next year, so San Jose needs to push the chips in here and figure out the finances next summer. Would the team be willing to trade blue-chip goaltending prospect Yaroslav Askarov to the Jets? San Jose may also need to sweeten a trade package -- or involve a third team -- in order to get Winnipeg to take on Logan Couture's contract.

Yes, Vegas is currently $8.6 million over the salary cap, so there would need to be some impressive maneuvering in order to acquire Hellebuyck. But the Golden Knights have already proven to be cutthroat if a player they covet hits the trade market. Besides, goaltending was optional in Sin City last season. Four goalies combined to allow 23.2 goals above average. Only five teams had a worse save percentage than the Golden Knights.

So, how could the Golden Knights pull off a Hellebuyck blockbuster? Trading an injured Alex Pietrangelo and his contract would help, but that may be costly. Veteran defenseman Brayden McNabb only has a modified no-trade clause, and the same is true for forwards Tomas Hertl, William Karlsson and Ivan Barbashev. Like I said, this would be tough, but the Golden Knights are one team willing to drop the entire egg carton on the floor to make a few omelettes.

#2724. Luka Dončić, Lakers stay hot offensively in win over Heat

The Lakers had a red-hot offensive night against the Heat on Monday to pick up a second straight victory, downing Miami 136-115.

LA shot 56.8% from the field and hit 19 3-pointers at a 44.2% clip. They had 39 assists on 51 made shots and dominated the paint, outscoring Miami 58-38.

LA quickly took a 10-point lead on the shoulders of Luka Dončić, who was already in double figures with 12 points. The Heat cut the deficit to two with Davion Mitchell and Klay Thompson combining for 11 points.

Walker Kessler had six points for Los Angeles.

Despite hot shooting from the field, the Lakers couldn't build much of a cushion. Giannis Antetokounmpo now led the Heat with eight points. Sandro Mamukelashvili provided a nice spark off the bench with five points.

The purple and gold were up seven at the end of the first.

Miami started the second period with the first four points before Austin Reaves drained a triple. The shots from behind the arc started to fall for Los Angeles with Matisse Thybulle and Ziaire Williams each knocking one down.

Miami cut the deficit all the way to one thanks to Giannis continuing to have a dominant first half as he was up to 17 points. As a team, the Heat were shooting 88% from the field.

LA's bench put in the work, combining for 27 points. Mamu led the way with nine. Much of the rest of the half remained a back-and-forth affair. The purple and gold went into the locker room up seven after shooting 67% from the field while Miami shot 59%.

Los Angeles also held a 36-24 advantage over the Heat in points in the paint.

Luka and Austin led the second period early, scoring nine points combined and forcing a quick Miami timeout. Out of the break, the Heat turned the ball over, leading to a layup from Kessler on the other end.

The star duo of Luka and Reaves continued to lead the way for LA, combining for 11 points, extending Los Angeles' momentum throughout the quarter. Williams's first game back from injury was stellar as he had nine points and two assists.

Bam Adebayo remembered he could play basketball and entered double figures with 11 points, but it didn't matter much as the Lakers still had all the momentum. They ended the third up 18. Luka had 37 points.

The final frame saw the Lakers start by scoring four in a row, but Tim Hardaway Jr. attempted to help Miami come back by draining two triples. It didn't matter as LA continued to shoot at an excellent rate from behind the arc, with Luka, LaRavia, Reaves and Mamu all knocking down threes.

Los Angeles subbed in its bench with 1:22 left, and they kept the lead this time without making it unnecessarily interesting.

Luka finished with 42 points, seven rebounds and 12 assists. Reaves ended with 27 points and five assists while shooting 10-15 from the field. Kessler notched 15 points with 15 rebounds.

In his return from injury, Williams poured in nine points off the bench. Mamu pitched in with 13 points and four assists.

The rest of the role players all had positive impacts in small ways across the board. Thybulle scored six points with two assists, Grimes had seven points with four assists, Collin Sexton logged six points and LaRavia finished with seven points, four rebounds, two assists and two blocks.

The Lakers' next game will be against the Sacramento Kings on Wednesday at 7:00 PM PT.

#2723. Avalanche sign star Cale Makar to largest contract in NHL history at $163.2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This has been the summer of spending in the NHL, and the Colorado Avalanche just broke the bank for star defenseman Cale Makar. On Friday, the team announced that Makar signed an eight-year extension worth $163.2 million.

The contract is the richest in league history -- both in total value and annual value at $20.4 million per year. Makar is the first player in NHL history to cross the $20 million salary threshold.

At 27-years old, Makar is arguably the best defensemen in the NHL, and he will remain in that conversation for quite a while. Makar has already won the Norris Trophy twice, and he was a key factor in Colorado's Stanley Cup run, which ended with him winning the Conn Smythe Trophy.

This past season, Makar posted monster numbers from the blue line yet again as he tallied 20 goals and 59 assists in 75 games. Since entering the NHL in 2019, Makar leads all defensemen in goals (20) and points (507).

"I am so excited and humbled to continue to wear the Avalanche sweater and represent this incredible organization and community," Makar said in a statement. "I would like to thank the Kroenke family, Joe Sakic and the entire Avalanche organization for their commitment, trust and belief in me. I would also like to thank my wife and family for their constant support, as well as Scott, Brian and Steve Bartlett for their guidance and assistance.

"To the Avalanche fans, thank you for your continued support and for welcoming us to Colorado years ago. Colorado has truly become a second home to us, and we are so grateful to be here. I look forward to getting back on the ice with my teammates and continuing to work toward our goal of bringing the Stanley Cup back to the Mile High City."

Over the last three seasons, Makar's impact has been immense in all three zones. He's posted a five-on-five expected goals share of 54.5%, per Natural Stat Trick. With Makar on the ice in those situations, Colorado has outscored its opponents 220-157. In two of the last three seasons, Makar has hit the 90-point mark, and he has 100-point potential at his best.

Makar's $11.4 million raise kicks in in at the start of the 2026-27 season, and it will make things significantly tighter for the Avalanche as they navigate the salary cap. The bright side for Colorado -- and the key in getting this deal done -- is that the team now has each of its core players signed through at least 2031.

There may be some sticker shock upon seeing the $20.4 million average annual value, but that's the new reality in the NHL as the cap rises exponentially. The previous record for highest salary in NHL history was just set earlier this offseason when the Anaheim Ducks signed center Leo Carlsson to a contract worth $18 million per year, and the Chicago Blackhawks announced a $75 million extension for Connor Bedard.

The next domino to fall will be an extension for Minnesota Wild defenseman Quinn Hughes, who is neck-and-neck with Makar as the best defensemen in the world. Waiting until after the Makar deal was announced to sign Hughes could prove to be a mistake for Wild general manager Bill Guerin.

#2722. Jeffery Simmons stellar in Bears debut: Winners, losers of Chicago's rout of Seahawks

If the Week 8 finale between the Chicago Bears and Seattle Seahawks served as an NFC championship game preview ... then hopefully the NFC championship game is much more entertaining.

Regardless, the Bears' 34-17 defeat of the reigning champion Seahawks on Monday, Nov. 2, at Lumen Field had something of a January feel as two eminently capable crews try to dial in for the second half of the season while integrating and reintegrating several key components. Chicago, which improved to 6-2 and is now within a half-game of the NFC North lead, currently looks like the more formidable side − now 4-0 in games that QB Caleb Williams starts and finishes. And while Seattle (4-4) might have retreated to .500 − and already suffered more losses than it did in 2025 − the Super Bowl 60 winners caught fire after a 3-2 start a year ago. Still, this was their first loss of 2026 by more than three points.

What does it all appear to mean in the moment? Your winners and losers from "Monday Night Football" in the PNW:

The Bears confirmed their own belief that they're serious contenders after last week's trade for All-Pro DT Jeffery Simmons. Wearing the No. 99 jersey once used by Hall of Famer Dan Hampton with the legendary '85 Bears, Simmons had a whale of a debut in navy and orange, racking up six tackles, two tackles for losses and a sack as Chicago's ninth-ranked defense seems poised to take a step up in class. Simmons, whose victorious night matched the number of wins he'd experienced with the Tennessee Titans in 2026, certainly had a more notable night in his new uniform than perennial All-Pro G Quenton Nelson, who was making his Seattle debut after also being dealt last week.

He's now 3-0 since returning from his three-game absence while healing from a hamstring injury. The top pick of the 2024 NFL Draft also became the first quarterback to pass for more than 200 yards against Seattle's top-ranked "Dark Side" defense this season. Williams, once again, also did a nice job distributing the ball with five of his receivers making multiple receptions after the Bears began the game as the only team in the league with five players who had at least 20 receptions on the season.

Now in his second season with the Seahawks, the veteran wideout caught his first regular-season TD pass in Seattle since 2019 … when Kupp was a member of the rival Los Angeles Rams.

While we Gen-Xers love the Phil Collins throwback sounds every week, mixing in The Bangles' "Manic Monday" was a nice touch.

They come out of their bye with a 2½-game lead over both the Seahawks and Rams in what was expected to again be the league's most competitive division – though the upstart Arizona Cardinals (3-5) are now much closer to the 'Hawks and Rams. And with a 3-0 division record, the Niners' advantage is actually even more significant.

The Colts won, 19-17, for their first win of the season.

Chicago entered the night with the league's second-ranked rushing attack – and only because the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' 324-yard output in Sunday's win during a Florida deluge skewed the Bucs into the lead. But they will remain there after the Bears RBs ran for all of 86 yards and 2.7 per carry – though a 39-yard lateral from Williams to WR Kalif Raymond made the final total (126 yards) look more respectable. And D'Andre Swift did wind up in the end zone three times.

Seattle got its top RBs, Zach Charbonnet (back from a torn ACL in last season's playoffs) and rookie Jadarian Price (back from a chest injury that landed him on injured reserve), on the field together for the first time. They're going to need time to grow after combining for just 52 rushing yards – and behind a reconfigured offensive line starting Nelson at left guard while Grey Zabel shifted to right guard and LT Charles Cross was missing entirely.

For a while, it appeared the PAT the Seahawks kicker missed and field-goal try that was blocked would loom large. Ultimately, that wasn't the case – but not a pretty night, from several aspects, for Seattle's typically solid special teams.

A quarterback who's had a notably uneven career is having that kind of season in microcosm. Behind his new-look line, Darnold was often under fire and consequently inaccurate, completing just half of his 34 passes for 188 yards, two TDs and another pick (his ninth in seven 2026 starts). Darnold doesn't need to be Seattle's leading man most weeks, but he's got to be more than a small-time character actor.
